THE CHINA MAIL.
BRITAIN'S VAST CREDIT.
ANSWER TO CRITICS.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer in the House of Commons yesterday refuted charges by the Labour Party that the return to gold is in any sense a gamble.
GOLD BAR SALES.
(Reuter's Service.)

In the House of Commons, the Financial Secretary of the Treasury, Lieutenant-Colonel W. Guinness, moving the second reading of the Gold Standard Bill pointed out in connection with the proposal that the Bank of England was bound to sell gold in amounts of not less than 400 eunecs troy fine gold in bar, that
CREDIT FOR BRITAIN
ERSTONE VIEW GO. NEW YOLA
each bar should be worth about $1,700, and the size of the bar alone would prevent this proposal being used to bring back gold into general use and limit the possible drawing of gold for export.

The clause of the Bill empowering the Treasury to borrow for exchange operations had not increased the total money to be borrowed. Any sums raised under these powers must come out of the usual provision for borrowing up to the total of the supply services for the year voted yearly in the Appropriation Act. Two credits had already been conditionally negotiated under this.

L.L. Col. Guinness said that credit had been arranged with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York who had undertaken to give the Bank of England a revolving credit of $200,000,000 for two years from May 10.
The second arrangement was with the syndicate beaded by Messrs. J. P. Morgan to His
ABOUR'S PROTEST
Mr. Philip Snowden, former Chancellor of the Exchequer, who led Labour attack on the back to gold policy.
Majesty's Government directs for a revolving credit of $100,000,000 also for two years.

The interest in each case was payable when the credit was drawn upon at one per cent. above the Federal Reserve discount rate with a minimum of four per cent. and a maximum of six per cent., or if the Federal Reserve rate should exceed six per cent. at the Federal discount rate.

Lt. Col Guinness hoped that in view of the urgency of the matter the House would pass the measure without delay. He did not fear a rise in the bank rate or higher prices.

The Government believed we had reached the stage of the purchasing power being at parity, and that in the long run the producer would have more gain from the security of the gold standard than the banking interest.
Labour's Protest.
Mr. Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer in the Labour Cabinet, moved a Labour amendment refusing to assent to the bill, which he said by providing for return to the gold standard
with undue precipitancy might aggravate the existing grave conditions of unemployment and trade depression.
Mr. Snowden emphasised that he did not oppose the return to the gold standard, but he protested against the Government's precipitancy.
The Labour Party, he said; by the amendment dissociated themselves from the disastrous consequences which might result. (Ministerial laughter.)

Mr. Snowden said he did not accept Mr. Churchill's statement of the existence of a practical parity between prices in Britain and the United States. He, Mr. Snowden, thought that the difference amounted to five per cent. The Government should have united a little longer in the hope that parity of the gold level and prices could be reached by the formal operation of trade.
Finest Expert Advice.

Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, denied that the decision was characterised by precipitancy. On the contrary, he said, they had secured the finest expert financial advice in the world. The Government had taken every precaution which forethought, patience and long preparation could suggest.

He mentioned the disadvantage of giving long notice of the return to gold and pointed out that if we had waited for the Act to expire at the end of the year everyone could under the existing law have withdrawn and hoarded gold against the date of free export, namely January, when the normal demand for bullion is high. He insisted that no country in the world was less able to afford diverging from economic facts than Britain. As regards the allegation that the decision would shackle them to America, the Chancellor said it would certainly shackle them to reality for good or ill. He personally believed it was the only basis offering permanent security.
Our Vast Credit.

Mr. Churchill knew of nothing which would justify as increase in the rate in the immediate future. Indeed the situation was stable and, everything tended to show that the transition to gold up to the present had been effected—he was not going to prophesy about the future—with great success.

Mr. Churchill declared that Britain was not only the financial centre of the world, she was the centre of a wide Empire. If we detached ourselves from their movements we ran a great risk of becoming isolated and loosening the bond, whereas the fortification thereof was indispensable to our well being.
Mr. Churchill scouted the suggestion we might be unable to hold our own against strong trans-Atlantic influences.
He poinied out that Britain still controlled a vast amount of the world's business and had magnificent credits, also £3,000,000,000 in foreign investments.
She held £153,000,000 in gold and the Dominions held £107,000,-000. The Empire supplied seventy per cent. of the world's gold.
An Enormous Power.
The House of Commons passed the second reading of the Gold Standard Bill without division.

Mr. Churchm cited instances of pre-war discrepancies in the British and American price levels and their normal timely readjustment in order to disprove that absolute equation of prices was essential to the restoration of the gold standard.

Mr. Churchill concluded by saying that the Dominions united were an enormous power. They were great, intricate and comprehensive enough to exist side by side in amicable association with an even larger economic financial power without their own essential independence being prejudicially affected.
GREAT WELCOME.
HAILED BY STUDENTS.
(Reuter's Scrolloe.)
Capetown, May 1.

The Prince of Wales motored to the Nationalist stronghold of Stellenbosch. He was welcomed enthusiastically, twenty-four stalwart young Dutch students hauling him in an open carriage a distance of two miles to the sports ground, where he addressed the assembled students of the local university.
SOUTH AFRICA'S PREMIER.

General Hertzong.
The Prince lunched at the agricultural Hall and afterwards notored to Huguenot Station where he joined the Royal train in which he makes his long trek.
Earlier Cables.
(Keuter's Service.)

At the dinner to the Prince of Wales, the Premier, General Hertzog was warmly applauded for his speech supporting the toast to His Royal Highness. He said the Prince would be welcomed equally and sincerely on the lovely plains of the Free State, and the high veldt of the Transvaal.
General Smuts said the South Africans loved the Prince's simplicity, human ways and sincerity. The people were deeply attached to him as heir apparent to the throne.
TIED HANDS.
BELGIUES POLITICAL
It is feared that deadlock which aided the balance of the Parties and deprived the country of a government for the past month can only be solved by another general election.

Since the Socialists have declared to form a homogeneous ministry, the Catholic Right has decided to form a bloc with the Conservatives and Christian Democrats, but a section of the Relds who could support either the Catholics or Socialists are determined not to share the responsibility of government while the Catholic clubs vehemently oppose a combination of Catholics and Socialists.
Fence all the parties have tied hands and the crisis is only soluble, part from fresh elections, by a cabinet composed of non-members of Parliament.
PROGRESS.

JAPANESE CONCESSION
BUND.
(By Courtesy of Daily Bulletin).
At a meeting of the Japanese community, it was decided that a new band for the Japanese Concession be constructed at an estimated cost of $1,000,000.
The meeting authorised the Council to approach the Japanese Foreign Office for a loun totalling Yen 500,000, the reminder to be obtained from the banks.
When, the new international bridge is completed by the end of 1926, steamers will be able to berth at the proposed bund, which it is hoped will be completed then.
INDIA'S HOPE.

Tenders have already been invited.
The Japanese Consul-General estimates that foreign firms will be asked to submit tenders.
CONDITIONAL CO-OPERATION PROPOSALS.
“Unable to Hurl Defiance at the British Throne.”
Mahatma Ghandi, whose personality is probably the greatest single factor in the politics of India today, has resumed his old position following his release from jail.

Gandhi in the course of a long speech announced that the differences had been amply settled.

SHOTS IN A POLLING BOOTH.
TWO PEOPLE KILLED.
(Reuter's Service.)

The final results of the municipal elections are not expected until to-night at the earliest, but the fact emerges that the Left Cartel have gained advantages while the Communist have had severe setbacks.
Second polls are necessary in a number of cases.
The only disturbing incident occurred in Corsica, where shots were fired inside a polling station. Two people were killed and three injured.
MAYOR AGAIN.
M. Herriot, former Premier, who has been elected Mayor of Lyons again.
Earlier Cables.
(Havia Agency.)
Paris, May 4.
The municipal elections show that no change has taken place in Paris. Forty-eight definite results are recorded and 31 second ballots will be required.

Gandhi added that 'freedom could only be attained by Hindu and Mostern unity, the removal of untouchability, and the adoption of the spinning wheel.

The conference unanimously passed a resolution condemning both the revolutionary methods and the Bengal Ordinance and expressing faith in the innocence of those detained as suspects under the Act of 1818 unless the contrary were proved at open trial.

The 'Swarajist' outlook was surveyed by the leader, Mr. C. R. Das, in his presidential address before the Bengal Provincial Congress at Faridpur. Mr. Das said Swaraj was attainable within the British Empire because the Dominion status expresses and implies all the elements of Swaraj.

Mr. Das again condemned revolutionary violence, but said the co-operation invited by Lord Birkenhead is impossible in the present atmosphere of distrust. He declared that if the Swaraj's settlement was not responded to they must continue to make administration impossible and be prepared for ultimate civil disobedience; but he did not anticipate such a contingency, as he saw signs of reconciliation everywhere.

In Lyons, M. Herriot, the Mayor, was re-elected with 28 Left Blockists and 28 second ballots required.
In Marseilles 28 Left Blockists were elected with eight second ballots required: In Bordeaux 23 Left Blockists were elected and thirteen second ballots needed:
Several great towns show no definite results. In Metz and Rouen' no Left Blockists were elected. Everywhere the Communists suffered severe losses.
BRAZIL'S CONGRESS OPENS.
RJO DE JANTITSO LOOKING TOWARD CAJUS ISLAND
Rio de Janeiro, May 4.

At the re-opening of Congress, the Premier stated that the budget deficit was 89,788 contos. Exports exceeded imports by £26,154,000. He pointed out the inadequacy of the Navy and emphasised the necessity for purchasing three cruisers, 15 destroyers and 10 submarines in the course of a number of years. — Reuter's American Service.
